title: The Calendar: Sun, Moon and the Year
lead: How the Bible and its readers reckon time: days, weeks, months and years. God made the lights of the sky to "mark the appointed times, the days and the years" (Genesis 1:14), but the Bible never gives the rules of the calendar. Israel's months followed the moon; some Jews in the centuries before Jesus, following 1 Enoch and Jubilees, insisted on a 364-day year of exactly 52 weeks, and the dispute shaped the Dead Sea Scrolls.

sections.b: The Bible's months are moon months: the Hebrew chodesh, "month," means "new moon," and new moons had their own offerings (Numbers 28:11–15). The year began in spring, in the month of Passover (Exodus 12:2), and the feasts were tied to the harvest (Exodus 23:14–17; Leviticus 23). The Bible never says how the moon months were kept in step with the seasons; later Jews did it by adding a thirteenth month in some years. Psalm 104:19 says God "made the moon to keep the appointed times," and Sirach makes the moon the sign of the feasts (Sirach 43:6–8). The New Testament mentions feast days, new moons and Sabbaths, and warns believers not to judge one another over them (Colossians 2:16; Galatians 4:10; Romans 14:5–6).

sections.b: 1 Enoch's Astronomical Book (chapters 72–82, from the 200s BC or earlier) teaches a year of twelve 30-day months plus four added days: 364 days, exactly 52 weeks, so every date falls on the same weekday every year. Jubilees makes it a command and condemns those who follow the moon (Jubilees 6:32–38), and many Dead Sea Scrolls use it. The real year is about 365¼ days, so the scheme drifts unless corrected; whether and how its users corrected it is unknown. Most scholars think the temple in Jerusalem, like the later rabbis, kept a moon calendar with added months; some, such as VanderKam, think the 364-day year was once the temple's own priestly calendar.

Christians kept the week and Sunday, the day of the resurrection (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and from early on argued over the date of Easter, which follows the moon of Passover. The Council of Nicaea (325) set a common rule, and churches still differ in how they apply it: Western churches use the Gregorian calendar, many Orthodox churches the older Julian one. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church keeps the Alexandrian year of 365 days (366 in leap years), with twelve months of 30 days and a short thirteenth month, and reckons its moveable feasts by its own computus (baḥrä ḥassab). None of the churches uses the 364-day year of 1 Enoch.
